set.name: Asmalı Meyhane
set.hook: A 1950 meyhane on the bazaar street, grilling island squid and serving raw fish with basil.
set.why: Niko Manalodis and his brothers opened it in 1950, and the house still cooks the island way: kalamar laid on the coals rather than battered, and raw fish dressed with basil, the two plates Daily Sabah says you find only here. Yemek.com describes the room through its details: painted stairs, a resident cat and an old record player, with a meze counter of walnut octopus, fennel cuttlefish and stuffed courgette flowers.
set.verdict: Order the grilled kalamar and the raw fish and let the counter choose the rest; that is where the kitchen is strongest. Online reviews are mixed, with praise for the meze and the staff and complaints about price and slow service at busy times. Go early in the evening, before the summer crowd fills the stairs.
set.signature: Grilled island kalamar, then raw fish with basil.
set.caveat: No 2026-dated evidence and no winter dates found; reviews mention high prices and uneven service on busy nights.

set.hook: A meze house inside Apostol Kalfa's old coffeehouse, on the street that was once the island bazaar.
set.why: The street was the centre of the Bozcaada bazaar, and the building was the coffeehouse of Apostol Kalfa, an islander. When it became a restaurant the owners kept what was left: tall guillotine window frames no one on the island makes any more, a hand-planed ceiling and cedar floorboards. Tables spill under vines and flowers outside. The meze list runs to island herb salad, the house borani and mastic-scented artichokes.
set.verdict: Yemek.com calls it an island classic, and every guide we found sends you here for the meze and the squid rather than for a view. It is a lane, not a harbour terrace. Evenings are hard to get even in September and October, so book days ahead in season and call to confirm it is open out of season.

set.hook: A family home-cooking kitchen started by retired teachers, known for its mantı.
set.why: Retired primary-school teachers opened it more than forty years ago, and it still cooks like a house kitchen: dolma and vine-leaf sarma that diners compare with a grandmother's, stuffed courgette flowers in season, and the mantı people come back for, pinched small and served with yoghurt. set.verdict: Come for lunch and the mantı; it is the reason to cross town, and the olive-oil vegetables are the reason to stay. Do not expect a sea view or a fish grill. The evidence is reviews without dates, so treat the details as likely rather than certain, and check it is open before planning around it.

set.name: Talay Şarapçılık
set.hook: Family winery since 1948, pouring native-grape wines at a paid tasting counter in the town shop.
set.why: In 1948 the brothers Necati, Hayati and Sebati Talay started making wine on the island; bottling followed in 1955, and today the firm makes about 600,000 litres a year, two-thirds of it from the family's own grapes. You do not drive out to vines here: you walk into a sales shop in town, line up bottles of Vasilaki, Karalahna and Kuntra on the counter and pay for a small flight, the way islanders buy wine for the table.
set.verdict: The plainest way to taste Bozcaada's own grapes without a car or a booking: a working family producer, not a showpiece estate. Expect a shop counter rather than a cellar tour, and modest prices against the boutique labels. Whether the counter keeps winter hours is not published anywhere we could find, so treat a November visit as a phone call first.
set.signature: A paid flight at the town shop, ending on the Cabernet Sauvignon-Kuntra red
set.caveat: A sales shop, not a cellar tour; no published winter hours found, call before going in November-April

set.hook: The architect's estate at Tuzburnu that made Bozcaada a name in serious wine; Çavuş white, Corpus red.
set.why: Reşit Soley gave up architecture for vines and named his winery after the crows that crowd the island. The estate sits at Tuzburnu Bay, working Kuntra, Karalahna, Çavuş and Vasilaki beside Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah. Its flagship, Corpus, is about two-thirds Cabernet, and JancisRobinson.com has reviewed several vintages of it. On the property, the Wine and Bite shop-café pours by the glass with the vineyard in view.
set.verdict: The island's most internationally reviewed label and the bottle to open if a guest wants proof that Bozcaada can make a serious wine. It is also the dearest: one visitor found the island shop dearer than Ankara retail. Visiting has long been seasonal (a 2009 guide gave June to September for cellar tastings), and we found no current winter schedule, so do not plan an off-season visit without a reply from the winery.

set.caveat: Estate outside town; tastings historically summer-only (June-September in 2009); no 2026 winter hours found; island prices can exceed city retail

set.name: Amadeus MMX
set.hook: A small Austrian family winery that grows Grillo and Croatian Žlahtina beside native Vasilaki.
set.why: The Gareis family came to Turkey from Austria in the 1960s; Oliver Gareis, born on the island, began making wine as a hobby in 2010, the MMX on the label. His father brought back Grillo from the Mediterranean and Žlahtina from the island of Krk, and the blog Quirky Cork says this is the only place in Turkey growing Žlahtina. They grow beside the native Vasilaki, and the Cuvée Blanche blends all three with Sauvignon Blanc.
set.verdict: Go for the host and the oddities: grapes you will not taste anywhere else in Turkey, poured by the man who planted them, and bottles that are hard to find even in Istanbul. Lonely Planet rates the Cabernets. It is a small operation outside town with no published visiting hours, and nothing we found says it receives visitors in winter, so message ahead.
set.signature: The Cuvée Blanche, then the Grillo with the island's vegetable and fish mezes
set.caveat: Small family cellar outside town, own transport needed; no published hours or winter opening found; message before going

set.name: Bozcaada Wednesday Market
set.hook: The island's weekly market day: fruit, vegetables, cheese and jars of tomato jam bought from the grower.
set.why: Once a week the island's growers set out what the souvenir shelves resell: tomatoes, fruit and, in late summer, the Çavuş grapes the island registered as a geographical indication in 2020. Around the castle square, stalls stack jars of tomato and fig jam, garlic confit and the almond-mastic cookies of the old Greek kitchen. The castle walls are the backdrop the tourist board still photographs.
set.verdict: The one place to buy island produce from the person who grew it, and the best shopping stop for a galley. But the details are soft: most sources say Wednesday, one says Friday, and Katie Parla noted the weekly market had moved without saying where. Ask at the harbour or the municipality which day and square it uses this winter before planning around it.
set.signature: Domates reçeli (tomato jam) with a wedge of local goat cheese
set.caveat: Day and site disputed (Wednesday in most sources, Friday in one; Parla reports it moved); winter running not confirmed; bring cash

set.hook: Wood-fired pastane: mastic-almond cookies, island breakfasts, fig, mastic and lavender ice cream.
set.why: The pastries go into a stone oven over a wood fire, and the recipes, the shop says, come from the kitchens of the island's Rum families. The almond cookie scented with mastic is the same one baked on Gökçeada and in Kavala. Şermin Günday kept the shop going after her husband died and added Tahir Usta to the name; the ice-cream counter next door rotates flavours weekly, mastic, wild fig and lavender among them.
set.verdict: The island's breakfast-and-sweets stop, worth it for the cookie and the fig ice cream, not as a meal. It has not been touched by the chains. The catch is the calendar: one Hürriyet column describes the island shop as the family's summer branch, so in November it may be shut. Check before promising guests an ice cream.
set.signature: Damla sakızlı bademli kurabiye, plus a scoop of wild-fig or mastic ice cream
set.caveat: Counter and breakfast place, not dinner; the island branch may be summer-only (Hürriyet), ice-cream flavours rotate and are seasonal

v03-cicek-pastanesi.evidence: Search extracts only, no 2026-dated source. Hürriyet (Ebru Erke column, undated): Şermin Günday kept the business after her husband's death and added 'Tahir Usta' to the name; extract says her daughter runs a summer location on the island, separate from her mainland shop. Gazete Vatan ('Bir yaz klasiği Bozcaada'): breakfasts and pastries, stone oven and wood fire, recipes from Bozcaada's Rum kitchens. Yemek.com (En İyi 10 Bozcaada Mekanı): in the Rum quarter; mastic-almond cookie tradition of nearly 150 years; attached ice-cream shop with weekly rotating flavours. Tours Around Turkey: mastic, wild fig and lavender ice cream. Katie Parla (undated extract): 'still going strong'. No source for 1959.
corrections: Old 'baking since 1959': no source found; dropped from copy. Sources speak instead of a near-150-year recipe tradition
Old 'run by Tahir Usta's children, the Günday family': Hürriyet says Şermin Günday runs it after her husband's death and added Tahir Usta to the name; daughter runs the island summer branch
Old location 'Çınar Çarşı by Alaybey Mosque': Yemek.com puts it in the Rum quarter; old pin dropped
Old 'year-round' implication: island shop may be summer-only
